content: Newborn admission temperature is a critical predictor of outcomes across all gestational ages. Hypothermia immediately after birth remains a global concern, and prolonged hypothermia is associated with significant harm. Maintaining normothermia in preterm infants is challenging, even when adhering to recommended thermal care guidelines in the delivery room. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of interventions aimed at preventing hypothermia in preterm and/or low birth weight infants when applied within 10 minutes of birth in the delivery room. These interventions were compared to routine thermal care or other single or combined interventions designed for the same purpose. The review included 25 studies across 15 comparison groups. These were categorized into three main types of interventions: barriers to heat loss, external heat sources, and combinations of interventions. Barriers to Heat Loss: The use of plastic wraps or bags, compared to routine care, significantly improved core body temperature on admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) or up to two hours after birth. The mean difference in temperature was 0.58°C (95% CI 0.50 to 0.66), based on 13 studies involving 1,633 infants. Additionally, fewer infants experienced hypothermia on admission to the NICU (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.72; NNTB 4, 95% CI 4 to 5). However, the use of plastic wraps was associated with an increased risk of hyperthermia (RR 3.91, 95% CI 2.05 to 7.44; NNTH 25, 95% CI 17 to 50). Despite this, fewer infants in the plastic wrap group had temperatures outside the normothermic range (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.81; NNTH 5, 95% CI 4 to 7). There was insufficient evidence to suggest that plastic wraps or bags significantly reduced the risk of in-hospital mortality or major morbidities, except for a reduction in the risk of pulmonary hemorrhage. Evidence regarding variations of this approach is limited, as it is based on findings from only one or two small studies. External Heat Sources: Emerging evidence supports the use of external heat sources, such as skin-to-skin care (SSC) and thermal mattresses, in reducing hypothermia risk. One study involving 31 infants demonstrated that SSC was effective in reducing hypothermia risk compared to conventional incubator care for infants with birth weights between 1,200 and 2,199 grams (RR 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.64; NNTB 2, 95% CI 1 to 4). Thermal mattresses significantly improved core body temperature in infants weighing ≤1,500 grams (MD 0.65°C, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.94) and reduced the incidence of hypothermia on NICU admission. No significant increase in hyperthermia risk was observed. Combinations of Interventions: Two studies (77 infants) compared thermal mattresses to plastic wraps or bags in infants born at ≤28 weeks' gestation. No significant differences were found in core body temperature, hypothermia incidence, hyperthermia incidence, or temperatures outside the normothermic range on NICU admission. Two additional studies (119 infants) compared the combination of plastic bags and thermal mattresses to plastic bags alone in infants born at <31 weeks' gestation. Meta-analysis showed improved core body temperature on NICU admission or up to two hours after birth, but an increased risk of hyperthermia. No significant differences were observed in the risk of temperatures outside the normothermic range or other reported morbidities. Conclusions: Moderate-quality evidence indicates that plastic wraps or bags, compared to routine care, result in higher admission temperatures and reduced hypothermia, particularly in extremely preterm infants. Thermal mattresses and SSC also reduce hypothermia risk, but findings are based on limited studies. Caution is necessary to avoid iatrogenic hyperthermia, especially when multiple interventions are used simultaneously. Limited evidence suggests that these interventions are beneficial and do not cause harm for most short-term morbidities associated with hypothermia, such as major brain injury, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity, necrotizing enterocolitis, and nosocomial infections. Observational studies have shown increased mortality in preterm infants with hypothermia compared to those maintaining normothermia. However, evidence is insufficient to conclude that these interventions reduce in-hospital mortality across all comparison groups. Hypothermia may serve as a marker of illness and poorer outcomes rather than a direct cause. Limitations: The review was limited by the small number of identified studies, small sample sizes, and variations in methods and definitions of hypothermia, hyperthermia, normothermia, routine care, and morbidity. Most comparison groups lacked sufficient power to detect effects on morbidity and mortality. Future research should focus on adequately powered studies to detect rarer outcomes, apply standardized morbidity definitions, and assess longer-term outcomes, particularly neurodevelopmental outcomes.
